One of my Favorite Childhood Games Hasn't Aged Well [Age of Empires 2]

Very nice write-up; thank you for sharing!

After playing through a few older games I really started thinking about why some games have aged better than others. Was it on my end, had my tastes changed? Or am I older now, do I understand the basics of game design better now? After some serious thought on this I’ll do my best to work through this.

This is a sensation that I've always recognized but could never quite put my finger on. In my case I honestly think that I'm just less forgiving on games in retrospect than I was when I first played them. With my first experience playing a new game, I'm usually blown away by the good aspects of that game that I overlook the bad. Games improve and influence each other, and I start to take those good aspects for granted because they're only innovations when viewed in context of when they were created. Replaying old games I notice the negatives more than those aged innovations, and I'm less forgiving on the impact they have on my gameplay experience.

That's something that the article came back and touched on towards the end, and I'm glad that it was included along with the other potential factors at play. One thing is for sure: if a game is good enough to make you dust off the cobwebs, there must be something there that you still treasure after all :)

For me, it's partially that I have so many more options now. I had the game that I rented for the weekend, or my other 5 games that I'd already beaten back then. Now I have a steam backlog of >100 games. If I get bored, it's super-easy to move on, so I'm less forgiving of flaws.
That's a really good point as well. When I had a PS1 I had literally five games and you can be sure I played and enjoyed them to death :P

And yet I could pick up MGS1 for PS1 tomorrow and have an excellent experience. That one might be my nostalgia, though, because that game was one of three that year (along with Halflife1 and Zelda 64) that totally changed my concept of gaming, and arguably changed gaming itself.
I whole-heartily agree. Half-life and MGS defined in my mind what gaming could be.
It was an amazing year for gaming, and if I remember Fallout 2 also came out that year (or within a couple months). Giants were born that year whose impact is still being felt.

It's fucking old. Pardon me if I don't understand the point of this review. Isn't comparing an RTS from the 1990s to StarCraft 2 like comparing apples to oranges? Of course the game play is slow. Computers were slow back then! Maybe I'm just being bitchy.

It's not a review of the game, it's a introspective thought-piece on growing up and being nostalgic. In this case the author chose to use the game, but it could have been his favorite movie from when he was a kid, or even a place he used to go.

It's not incredibly deep, but it's mos-def not about the game.

Regardless of your question not really being in line with the point of the article, many old games are still viable despite their age. For instance, the original XCOM is arguably still the best alien invasion simulation tactics/management game (though I would argue that Xenonauts might actually be better now, if age and graphics are totally discounted). Homeworld is from 1999 but has yet to be outdone, hence a remake that amounts to little more than a graphic upgrade. Ultima Underworld and System Shock are older than AoE2 and are still, despite clunky controls and UIs, two of the best firstperson RPGs ever made.

The RTS genre, unfortunately, is full of games that are so similar in design that it is hard for many of them to stand out. So many clones came out, especially after Warcraft 2 was a megahit, that they started to kind of all blur together. AoE was like that for me, I just didn't see the point. After the market was saturated in the mid and late 90s with standard RTS games that were all almost identical I gave up on the genre entirely until Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War in 2004 with a slightly different template.

Anyway, just cause games are old doesn't mean they suck is my point, whippersnapper.
